name: Indoor Air Quality
author: @opensmell
tagline: Live indoor air context from the sensors you actually have.
summary: An indoor air quality workspace for rigs with CO2, VOC, temperature, humidity, or particulate channels. It translates live sensor readings into ventilation and exposure context, tracks trends, and keeps the limits explicit: it is not a certified AQI monitor, not a medical device, and not a substitute for calibrated reference instruments.
scope: Support repeated indoor air decisions: when to ventilate, when to inspect a source, and when to log a change. Use it on the same rig, with known sensors, and treat readings as operational context rather than regulatory measurements.
limits: Not a certified air quality monitor, medical device, or regulatory compliance instrument. Do not use it for life-safety, legal, or clinical decisions.

Sensor readings depend on calibration, placement, warmup, humidity, cross-sensitivity, and sensor age. A low reading does not prove air is safe; a high reading does not identify the specific contaminant.

CO2, VOC, PM, temperature, and humidity are different measurements. This workspace does not convert them into an official EPA AQI unless your rig has the required calibrated pollutant sensors and a validated mapping.
citations: World Health Organization. WHO global air quality guidelines: particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide. 2021.
ASHRAE Standard 62.1, Ventilation for Acceptable Indoor Air Quality. Use the current edition applicable to your jurisdiction and project.
US EPA. Air Quality Index (AQI) Basics. https://www.airnow.gov/aqi/aqi-basics/. Referenced to define official AQI; this workspace does not compute it.

widgets.headline: Air readings need context before action.
widgets.body: A sensor change can mean ventilation, occupancy, a source event, sensor drift, or humidity interference. Use this workspace to decide when to ventilate or inspect, then confirm with the appropriate primary measurement before making a safety or compliance claim.
always: Treat CO2, VOC, PM, temperature, and humidity as different measurements with different failure modes.
Let sensors warm up and record placement, calibration date, and known sources before comparing sessions.
Ventilate or remove people from obvious hazard situations first; do not wait for a dashboard score.
never: Do not present this as an EPA AQI, medical-grade, or regulatory compliance reading.
Do not treat a VOC index or MOX response as a specific chemical identification or concentration without calibration.
Do not ignore symptoms, alarms, or known hazards because the dashboard looks normal.

widgets.title: Air log
widgets.description: Record the context that changes interpretation: occupancy, ventilation, sources, and sensor state.

rules.when: CO2 rises above your ventilation target on a calibrated CO2 sensor
rules.then: Increase ventilation or reduce occupancy, then confirm the trend returns toward baseline.

rules.when: VOC or MOX response rises sharply without a known source
rules.then: Inspect for sources, ventilate, and do not identify the chemical from the array alone.

rules.when: A sensor is warming up, dead, saturated, or recently moved/calibrated
rules.then: Do not use its readings for decisions until it is stable and its status is understood.

rules.when: People have symptoms, a combustion/gas alarm triggers, or there is visible smoke/haze
rules.then: Follow safety procedure immediately. This workspace is not a life-safety system.

widgets.title: Use this with your rig
widgets.body: Connect a rig with CO2, VOC, temperature, humidity, or particulate channels. The workspace uses host-owned live readings and flags when the baseline is not ready. Compare recordings in Check on the same rig.

docs.title: How to use this workspace
body: Place sensors in the breathing zone or a representative location, away from direct vents, windows, sun, and point sources unless you are intentionally measuring a source.
Allow warmup. CO2 NDIR sensors can be usable quickly, but many MOX/VOC sensors need a stable warmup and baseline period before changes are meaningful.
Use trends and context together. A rising CO2 trend during occupancy usually means ventilation; a VOC spike after cleaning usually means a source event. Log the context before acting.

docs.title: What it cannot tell you
body: It cannot certify compliance with EPA AQI, WHO guidelines, OSHA limits, or building code. Those require appropriate calibrated instruments and methods.
It cannot identify a specific VOC or gas from an uncalibrated MOX response. Treat VOC signals as change indicators unless you have a calibrated target gas model.
It cannot make a room safe. Ventilation, source control, maintenance, and calibrated safety detectors are the primary controls.

docs.title: Sensor roles
body: CO2 (NDIR, e.g. SCD30/SCD4x): useful for ventilation and occupancy context. It is not a direct measure of all pollutants.
VOC/MOX (e.g. SGP30/SGP40/BME680/MQ135): useful for detecting changes and source events. Cross-sensitive to humidity, temperature, and many compounds.
Temperature and humidity: context channels. They affect comfort, sensor response, and interpretation.
Particulate matter (PM): if present, treat as a separate pollutant class. PM sensors need their own placement and cleaning considerations.
